claims.text: A continuous iron oxide film on Q235 steel provides partial corrosion protection at lower temperatures.
Above about 700 °C, aggressive chloride salts locally infiltrate the oxide film on Q235 steel.
Above about 700 °C, aggressive chloride salts partially dissolve the oxide film on Q235 steel.
High-temperature salt interaction promotes protective-scale spallation.
Breakdown and spallation of the protective scale cause accelerated corrosion of Q235 steel.
The tested material will be as-received Q235 steel with its mill scale removed and without prior heat treatment.
Q235 specimens will be exposed to chloride salts over temperatures ranging from ambient to 900 °C, with salt-free specimens as controls.
Repeated exposure cycles can be used to assess scale spallation.
Q235 develops a thin, initially protective iron oxide layer during exposure.
The stability and adhesion of the Q235 oxide layer are compromised by high-temperature salt interactions.
Molten-salt penetration or dissolution of the oxide permits direct attack on the underlying metal substrate.
Below approximately 700 °C, Q235 retains a relatively stable oxide film and corrosion remains near salt-free baseline levels.
Above approximately 700 °C, salt-exposed Q235 exhibits increased oxidation and scale spallation.
Above approximately 700 °C, salt-exposed Q235 has greater mass loss and poorer surface integrity than salt-free controls.
Salt-free Q235 exposed at the same temperatures forms a stable oxide layer with lower mass loss and minimal spallation.
The proposed mechanism applies to Q235 and similar carbon steels in chloride-rich environments above 700 °C under modest oxygen levels.
The proposed mechanism is not necessarily applicable to higher-alloyed or specially coated steels.
The hypothesis is falsified if the oxide remains intact without significant infiltration or spallation above 700 °C and mass-loss rates remain comparable to salt-free controls.

contradictions.description: The conditions require an identical salt load, while the intervention and baseline specify salt-free controls. Salt loading cannot literally be identical between salted and salt-free specimens unless the requirement is intended to apply only within the salt-exposed groups.
